support.locus: latin-perseus-latinlit (Cicero, Sallust, Caesar etc.; c. 240 hits)

cognate: OIr. tír ~ Lat. terra (both *ters- 'dry', specialised as 'dry land' only in Italic and Celtic); OIr. muir ~ Lat. mare (*mori-). Both members of the pair are exact cognates.
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes; Irish usually orders muir first ('for muir ⁊ tír'), Latin usually terra first ('terra marique'); Keating here has land first
shared_syntax: coordinated polar pair LAND + SEA used as a merism for 'everywhere'; in Irish both nouns governed by one preposition (for/ar/do muir ⁊ tír), in Latin coordinated ablatives (terra marique) or accusatives (maria ac terras)
context: Keating: Cellachán's relief force raised as 'sluagh do thír is sluagh do mhuir' (an army by land and an army by sea); the same formula runs through the Irish annals for expeditions ('slógad do muir ⁊ do thír'), matching the military use of Lat. terra marique (Cicero, Caesar, Sallust in the Perseus corpus). The slab's Latin anchors are not military: Plautus has the cosmic list 'mare terra caelum', Lucretius 'in mare de terris'. Old Irish has the pair in native heroic verse (Síaburcharpat Con Culainn: Cú Chulainn's hardships 'for muir ⁊ tír').
phrase: Italo-Celtic merism *móri- + *ters- 'sea and (dry) land' (OIr. for muir ⁊ tír ~ Lat. terra marique)
note: The land/sea polar expression is near-universal (Gk κατὰ γῆν καὶ θάλασσαν, Gmc 'land and sea' with other words), and Irish annalists knew Latin terra marique, so calque is possible; the Middle Welsh hits are in the Brut, which is translated from Latin. The only shared feature beyond the universal figure is that both languages fill it with the same two cognates, which follows from the Italo-Celtic specialisation of *ters- as 'land as opposed to sea'. Cited as a shared Italo-Celtic lexical pairing, not as proof of a PIE formula.

All 148 pivots are Keating's Foras Feasa ar Éirinn (Early Modern Irish prose history); partners are mostly late Greek prose (Galen, Plutarch), with some Menota, Latin, OHG and MBh. One low-confidence claim (muir/tír ~ mare/terra). Considered and rejected: BC-b2504 whiter-than-snow / blacker-than-coal (gual~kol, sneachta~snjór; the Irish comes from the Middle Irish crosáin description, the ON is a homily on Isaiah 1:18; generic); BC-bbe99 fear gonta ~ MBh para-vīra-hā (a basic collocation, different construction); the fír flathemon fertility passages (BC-77aa6, BC-a2c3c, BC-e4f75) have no congruent partner in the slab.
